assumptions: single dominant output pole
CL dominates the output-node capacitance
tradeoffs: increasing gm usually increases bias current and power
reducing CL is only valid when the real load permits it

assumptions: Miller compensation creates the dominant pole
the second pole and compensation zero are above UGF
tradeoffs: increasing Cc usually improves stability but reduces GBW and slew rate
increasing gm usually raises current and can reduce phase margin

assumptions: the dominant pole contributes approximately -90 degrees at UGF
one non-dominant pole dominates additional phase lag
no nearby zero materially changes phase
tradeoffs: lowering UGF can improve PM at the cost of speed
raising p2 can improve PM without intentionally sacrificing UGF

assumptions: first-order CTAT plus PTAT compensation
K is set by the topology-specific resistor/current ratio
tradeoffs: changing K changes both nominal Vref and first-order tempco
higher current can improve settling while increasing power and self-heating

assumptions: matched bipolar devices at current-density ratio N
series resistance and high-level injection are negligible
tradeoffs: larger N increases PTAT voltage but can increase area and mismatch sensitivity

assumptions: first-order temperature compensation
curvature and resistor tempco are handled separately
tradeoffs: a correct room-temperature Vref does not guarantee low tempco
residual curvature requires curvature compensation rather than unlimited ratio tuning

assumptions: error-amplifier input offset and feedback current are small
the loop has sufficient DC gain and the pass device has headroom
tradeoffs: larger divider resistance lowers quiescent current but raises noise and parasitic sensitivity

assumptions: the regulator remains in closed-loop regulation across the load sweep
tradeoffs: higher loop gain and a larger pass device improve load regulation but can increase area and complicate stability

ldo_loop_stability.equation: PM is measured from Spectre STB loopGain at the first 0 dB crossing
assumptions: the iprobe lies in the intended global feedback loop
zero-load and external-capacitance corners are evaluated separately
tradeoffs: more compensation can improve phase margin while reducing GBW and worsening load-transient recovery

assumptions: P and Q begin precharged to VDD
the latch devices remain off during the initial amplification phase
tradeoffs: larger input devices can increase gm but also raise input capacitance and kickback
more tail current can reduce delay while increasing energy and supply transients

assumptions: the cross-coupled NMOS transconductance is approximately constant
the small-signal regeneration model is used only after latch turn-on
tradeoffs: larger latch gm shortens regeneration but adds capacitance
larger output load increases delay and energy

assumptions: static power is negligible after regeneration
dynamic charge and discharge dominate average power
tradeoffs: larger devices improve matching or speed but increase switched capacitance
low average power does not imply low peak supply current

limitations: the topology uses PDK PNP and poly-resistor devices but dedicated BJT operating-point extraction is not implemented
mismatch, long-term drift, and resistor/BJT statistical models require dedicated Monte Carlo signoff
the paper's native-NMOS implementation is mapped to the active PDK LVT models and must be revalidated for input common-mode and startup headroom
the schematic uses ideal resistor values to preserve the published ratios; PDK resistor mapping and Monte Carlo mismatch require signoff
random offset and input-referred noise require mismatch Monte Carlo and transient-noise simulation
kickback and peak supply current require source impedance and interconnect parasitics
reset-state DC operating regions do not qualify dynamic regeneration
the first version uses an external verified reference input
the 1.8 V IO model names and voltage limits must come from an external PDK profile
load and line transient signoff requires package and routing parasitics
